content: The Signalboard release readiness review is scheduled for Thursday. The goal is to confirm alerts, digest generation, and the operator handoff before the demo.
Maya owns the operator handoff. She needs a short release digest that lists unresolved alerts and the next verification step.
The release digest is ready only when every open alert has an owner, a severity, and a verification command. Missing ownership blocks release readiness.
Alert routing separates critical deployment risk from routine follow-up. Critical alerts go to the on-call operator, while routine alerts appear in the next digest.
During the rehearsal, the build pipeline reported one medium severity alert: release notes were incomplete. Maya assigned the documentation owner and recorded a verification command.
Decision: keep the operator digest concise. It should show the release state, unresolved alerts, and the next action without reproducing full incident history.
The release readiness check passed after the documentation alert received an owner and verification command. The remaining routine alerts can be reviewed in the next planning cycle.
For the Console demo, search release readiness to show semantic recall, then inspect the related concept neighborhood and the code that builds the release digest.
The triage queue groups incoming alerts by service, severity, and release window. Each item is acknowledged, assigned, or deferred with a documented reason.
Critical alerts receive a fifteen-minute acknowledgement target. The on-call rotation is the default owner until a release lead accepts responsibility.
The demo dashboard should make a blocked release obvious before an operator reads the full alert list. The status chip and digest headline carry that decision.
A verification command is evidence, not a replacement for review. Operators record the command that confirms the alert is resolved and add a short result note.
The release coordinator checks the alert summary first, then opens the handoff only when the digest reports unresolved work.
Nora owns the notification integration. Her fallback is to write the digest to the local outbox when a webhook destination is unavailable.
The outbox keeps notification payloads local during rehearsal. Delivery state is shown as pending, delivered, or failed for operator follow-up.
The release window begins at 14:00 UTC. Routine alerts may continue after the window opens, but critical alerts require explicit release-lead approval.
The readiness score is informational. It summarizes verified checks but never overrides a blocking critical alert or an unassigned release risk.
The previous rehearsal found duplicate alert titles from two services. Deduplication now uses the service key, alert title, and active release window.
Decision: preserve the original alert title in the digest even after deduplication so the operator can match it to the source system.
The dependency check validates the API, worker, and notification adapter before the release digest is generated. Each check reports pass, warn, or fail.
A warning can ship with a named owner and a follow-up date. A failure blocks release readiness until the verification command succeeds.
Maya asked for a focused handoff view because the full event timeline made routine release review slower. The handoff now shows only active risks and next actions.
The incident timeline remains available for audit but is not rendered in the default digest. This keeps the release decision legible during an active handoff.
The release digest is generated from normalized alerts, dependency checks, and the current release window. It has no network dependency in demo mode.
The sample API exposes a health endpoint and a readiness endpoint. Both return synthetic state to keep the repository safe for demos and workshops.
For a clean recording, start from Overview, search release readiness, select a concept neighborhood, then open the code graph for build_release_digest.
The strongest Code Explorer moment is the path from the command line entry point through release orchestration to build_release_digest. Select the digest symbol after the graph settles.
The terminal beat should show marm-memory doctor first. It demonstrates that MARM is local and operational without exposing a user home directory or project checkout path.
If the recorder wants to run the sample app, open the terminal from demo-project and run python -m signalboard.cli. Crop the prompt if it reveals a local path.
The demo command prints a release-ready state, the unresolved alert count, and the next action. It is deliberately short enough to remain readable in a video edit.
The operator roster uses fictional names only: Maya for release coordination, Nora for notifications, and Rowan for dependency verification.
The release readiness story has three phases: intake alerts, verify dependencies, then hand off a concise digest. The graph should show those modules connected through the orchestration layer.
A successful rehearsal ends with one routine alert deferred to the next planning cycle. This gives the digest an honest next action instead of an unrealistically perfect state.
The final video should use the memory search, concept graph, code graph, and terminal dock as four views of the same local release-readiness workflow.

The sample repository has modules for intake, scoring, dependencies, delivery, and reporting. It is intentionally deeper than a single-script example so the code graph has several meaningful clusters.
The demo uses only synthetic release information. It makes a useful recording environment without requiring an account, network destination, private repository, or customer data.
